goal.objective:
`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two.

This task is a completion exercise: every file and function in this workspace already holds its final implementation except `digestBytes` in `src/digest.js`, whose body currently throws 'not implemented'. Implement only that function's body so it fulfills the specification above; keep its signature exactly as given, and do not edit any other file, export, or function. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

<system-reminder>
A skill is a reusable set of task-specific instructions. The following skills are available in this session:

<available_skills>
- `dsh-archive-agent-notes`: Use when adding, auditing, pruning, archiving, restoring, or reviewing Agent Notes in deepseek-harness; checks every new note for superseded active records, classifies implemented notes by future decision value, deletes rejected notes that no longer prevent a tempting fallacy, and applies the frozen archived/{kind} triplet and manifest rules.
- `dsh-code-review`: Use when reviewing a pull request in the deepseek-harness repo — orients the reviewer to this codebase's standards (AGENTS.md conventions, defensive patterns, ADRs, quality gates) and the review-specific checks that code alone can't show
- `dsh-doc-site-sync`: Use when publishing, updating, moving, or removing DeepSeek Harness documentation website pages; editing website/docs.ts mappings or navigation; diagnosing a page missing from the VitePress site; fixing projected documentation links; or running the docs:dev, docs:check, and doc-sync workflow after website-content changes.
- `dsh-doc-standards`: Use when writing, moving, reviewing, or auditing documentation in the deepseek-harness repo — choosing hierarchy and detail, separating tutorials from references, checking tutorial progression, trimming doc slop, responding to a verify-doc-budgets failure, or requests like "improve the docs", "audit the docs", "where should this be documented", or "this doc is too long".
- `dsh-find-simplifications`: Use when working in the deepseek-harness repo to find non-obvious simplification candidates, write proposed Agent Notes or inline TODO/FIXME/XXX notes, audit or coalesce superseded Agent Notes, or fold worthwhile simplification ideas from another PR; especially for dead, duplicated, speculative, over-built, added-then-removed, or hand-rolled-where-a-dependency-exists surfaces.
- `dsh-merging-stacked-prs`: Use when landing a stack of dependent GitHub PRs (A ← B ← C, where each bases on the one below) onto master, merging a PR whose base is another open PR's branch, or whenever a request mentions "stacked PRs", "PR stack", "dependent PRs", or merging several related PRs in sequence. Requires every same-repository dependency chain to use GitHub's official stacked-PR feature before landing so GitHub owns stack-wide rules, CI, ordering, retargeting, and merge state.
- `dsh-pre-push-checks`: Use before pushing, force-pushing, marking ready for review, or claiming checks pass on a deepseek-harness branch, and immediately after gh stack sync publishes rewritten branches, to select the smallest tests and checks that cover the outgoing or just-published diff without reflexively running the full repository suite.
- `dsh-prose-standard`: Use when writing, reviewing, restoring, trimming, or auditing prose in the deepseek-harness repo, including deciding where documentation or comments are required across Markdown, JSDoc, code and test comments, prompts, descriptions, diagnostics, and CLI or UI strings.
- `dsh-trim-cot-leakage`: Use when auditing or fixing prose that reads like a leaked reasoning transcript — dead design-session citations such as (decision N), audit item codes, or §N of uncommitted drafts; change narration such as "used to", "no longer", "this cut"; stack or review vantage ("a later PR in this stack", "rejected in review"); reviewer-addressed justifications; control-flow narration; or hedged planning residue in comments, JSDoc, docs, or Agent Notes.
- `record-browser-gif`: Record browser or Web UI interaction demos as optimized GIFs using the available built-in browser, state-based frame capture, and deterministic encoding, then publish to a dedicated assets branch when the task includes attaching the GIF to a pull request. Use when asked to make, record, or generate a GIF that demonstrates a browser workflow, and for every pull request that changes product-user-visible GUI behavior, which MUST include a GIF recorded from the pull request's real server and mode...
</available_skills>

If the user names a skill, or the task clearly matches a skill's description, call the `skill` tool with the exact skill name before taking task actions. Load all applicable skills, then follow their full instructions. This catalog contains summaries only; do not infer or follow a skill's instructions until it has been loaded.
A user may also invoke a skill directly; its <skill_content> block then appears in this conversation. Follow it, and do not call the `skill` tool again for that skill.
</system-reminder>

header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You implement one program task in the workspace you are given, against its own test suite, and you stop when the tests pass.

The workspace is your working directory: every bash command and every file path resolves inside it, so read and edit its files by their relative paths and never search outside it.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

2: 
3: A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
11: | `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
12: | `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |
13: 
14: `test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.
15: 
16: ## The task file
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.
19: 
20: ```
21: # build.tasks
22: task build node build.js
23: task bundle node bundle.js
24: needs bundle build
25: ```
26: 
27: `task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.
28: 
29: ## Modes
30: 
31: - `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
32: - `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
33: - `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.
34: 
35: ## Failures
36: 
37: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.
38: 
39: ## Known gaps
40: 
41: `order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

(End of file - total 41 lines)
</content>

| `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |

`test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.
One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.

`task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.
- `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
- `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.

- `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.

`order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

1: /** The snapshot reader and the staleness rule that decides what a plan runs. */
2: 
3: import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
4: import { digestBytes } from './digest.js'
5: import { order } from './graph.js'
6: 
7: const DIGEST = /^[0-9a-f]{8}$/
8: 
9: /** One refusal of a snapshot file, carrying the file and the 1-based line. */
10: export class SnapshotError extends Error {
11:   /**
12:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
13:    */
14:   constructor(message) {
15:     super(message)
16:     this.name = 'SnapshotError'
17:   }
18: }
19: 
20: /**
21:  * Read one snapshot file into the digests it records.
22:  * @param {string} path - the snapshot's workspace path, as the argument gave it.
23:  * @returns {Map<string, string>} the recorded digest of each path.
24:  * @throws {SnapshotError} when the file is unreadable or a line is malformed.
25:  */
26: export function readSnapshot(path) {
27:   if (!existsSync(path)) throw new SnapshotError(`cannot read snapshot ${path}`)
28:   const recorded = new Map()
29:   const lines = readFileSync(path, 'utf8').split('\n')
30:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
31:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
32:     const line = index + 1
33:     const text = raw.trim()
34:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
35:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
36:     if (words.length !== 2) throw new SnapshotError(`${path}: line ${line}: expected <path> <digest>`)
37:     if (!DIGEST.test(words[1])) throw new SnapshotError(`${path}: line ${line}: invalid digest ${words[1]}`)
38:     if (recorded.has(words[0])) throw new SnapshotError(`${path}: line ${line}: path ${words[0]} is recorded twice`)
39:     recorded.set(words[0], words[1])
40:   }
41:   return recorded
42: }
43: 
44: /**
45:  * Why one watched path makes its task stale, or undefined when it does not.
46:  * @param {string} path - the watched workspace path.
47:  * @param {Map<string, string>} recorded - the snapshot's digests.
48:  * @returns {string | undefined} the reason, as the plan line words it.
49:  */
50: function pathReason(path, recorded) {
51:   if (!recorded.has(path)) return `new ${path}`
52:   if (!existsSync(path)) return `missing ${path}`
53:   return digestBytes(readFileSync(path)) === recorded.get(path) ? undefined : `changed ${path}`
54: }
55: 
56: /**
57:  * Decide, for every task in run order, whether the plan runs it and why.
58:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[], reads: string[], writes: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
59:  * @param {Map<string, string>} recorded - the snapshot's digests.
60:  * @returns {{name: string, reason: string | undefined}[]} one decision per task, in run order.
61:  */
62: export function plan(tasks, recorded) {
63:   const running = new Set()
64:   return order(tasks).map((name) => {
65:     const task = tasks.get(name)
66:     const watched = [...new Set([...task.reads, ...task.writes])].sort()
67:     let reason
68:     for (const path of watched) {
69:       reason = pathReason(path, recorded)
70:       if (reason !== undefined) break
71:     }
72:     if (reason === undefined) {
73:       const stale = [...task.needs].sort().find(need => running.has(need))
74:       if (stale !== undefined) reason = `needs ${stale}`
75:     }
76:     if (reason !== undefined) running.add(name)
77:     return { name, reason }
78:   })
79: }

goal.objective:
`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two.
